analogy.p: Imagine a person holds a full pack of 52 cards made from two matching half-packs (one from each of their parents). Meiosis is like **copying the pack, shuffling, then dealing it out into four half-hands**, so each hand has one card from each matching pair, but the particular mixture is different each time. When two half-hands (gametes) are put together at fertilisation you get a new complete pack for a child. The analogy breaks down because the cards in a real pair are not identical (they carry different alleles) and real chromosomes are copied before being dealt, not just shuffled.
analogy.t: Shuffling and dealing a pack of cards

bullets: Meiosis happens in the **reproductive organs** (testes, ovaries; anthers, ovules).
The genetic information is **copied** first (DNA replication).
The cell **divides twice**, giving **four gametes**.
Each gamete has **a single set of chromosomes** (haploid: 23 in humans).
The gametes are **genetically different** from one another.
At **fertilisation** gametes fuse, restoring the **full number of chromosomes** (46) and mixing genes from two parents.
Know the body-cell numbers: human cells have **23 pairs of chromosomes**; one pair is the **sex chromosomes** (XX female, XY male).
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 8461 section 4.6.1.2 (Meiosis) says that cells in the reproductive organs divide by **meiosis** to form **gametes**. You must know that the genetic information is **copied**, the cell then **divides twice** to form **four gametes**, each with a **single set of chromosomes**, and that **all four gametes are genetically different** from each other. You must also know that **fertilisation restores the diploid number** and that the mixing of genes from two parents produces **variation**. Meiosis matters because it explains why siblings differ, why chromosome number stays constant across generations, and where new allele combinations come from.

bullets: **Chromosome**: a long coiled molecule of DNA found in the nucleus.
**Gene**: a section of DNA that codes for a protein; controls a characteristic.
**Allele**: a different version of the same gene (e.g. blue or brown eye colour alleles).
**Homologous pair**: the two chromosomes in a pair, same genes in the same order, possibly different alleles.
**Genome**: the entire genetic material of an organism.
**Diploid (2n)**: two sets of chromosomes; **haploid (n)**: one set.
Of each pair, one chromosome came from the **mother** and one from the **father**.
core.h: Chromosomes, genes and alleles: the vocabulary
core.p: Before meiosis makes sense you need the building blocks. The **nucleus** of a human body cell contains **23 pairs of chromosomes**. Each chromosome is a long molecule of **DNA** carrying many **genes**. A gene is a short section of DNA that codes for a particular **protein** and so controls a characteristic. The two chromosomes in a pair (one from each parent) carry the **same genes in the same places**, but they may carry different versions of a gene, called **alleles**. This is why the two chromosomes of a pair are not identical copies of each other.

bullets: Halving the chromosome number: 46 to 23 in each gamete.
Fertilisation: 23 (sperm) + 23 (egg) = 46 (zygote).
Without meiosis chromosome number would double every generation.
Meiosis ensures each gamete gets **one chromosome from each pair**.
Meiosis creates **genetic variation** through mixing alleles.
Meiosis is the only cell division that makes **haploid** cells; mitosis keeps cells diploid.
core.p: If a sperm with 46 chromosomes fused with an egg with 46 chromosomes, the zygote would have **92**, and the number would **double every generation**. Meiosis prevents this by **halving** the number of chromosomes in gametes so that **fertilisation restores** the diploid number. Meiosis also produces gametes that are **all different**, so that sexual reproduction generates **variation**.

bullets: **Step 1: DNA replication.** The cell grows and copies its genetic information; each chromosome now has two identical copies (chromatids).

**Step 2: first division.** Chromosome pairs (one from mum, one from dad) line up and the two chromosomes of each pair are pulled to opposite ends. This forms **two cells**, each with 23 chromosomes (each still has two copies).
**Step 3: second division.** In each of the two cells the copies of every chromosome are pulled apart, making **four cells**.
**Result:** four **haploid** cells (23 single chromosomes), all **genetically different**.
The cells then **differentiate** into gametes (sperm or egg) in animals or pollen/egg cells in plants.
**Fertilisation** later gives a diploid zygote, which divides by **mitosis**.
Exam shorthand: 'copy, divide, divide: four different haploid cells'.
core.h: The stages of meiosis step by step
core.p: Meiosis can be described in a simple sequence. A diploid cell in an ovary or testis first **copies its DNA**, so each chromosome now consists of two identical copies (sister chromatids) joined together. In the **first division** the chromosome pairs are **separated** so that each new cell receives one chromosome of each pair. In the **second division** the copies of each chromosome are **pulled apart**. The result is **four haploid cells**, each with a **single set of chromosomes**. Because the pairs line up and separate randomly, the four cells carry different mixtures of the parent's alleles.

bullets: Humans: **testes** (sperm) and **ovaries** (eggs).
Flowering plants: **anthers** (pollen grains) and **ovules** (egg cell).
Only some cells in these organs divide by meiosis; all other cells divide by mitosis.
Many gametes are made so that at least some reach fertilisation.
Gametes are specialised: sperm (tail, many mitochondria, enzymes in head); egg (large, food store, jelly coat).
The final stage of making a sperm is differentiation, not another division.
core.p: Meiosis does not occur in ordinary body cells; it happens only in **special cells of the reproductive organs**. In a male human, cells in the **testes** undergo meiosis continuously from puberty and make millions of **sperm**. In a female, cells in the **ovaries** begin meiosis and produce **egg cells**; in the human female, one large egg cell is produced from each meiosis in the cycle (the others are small cells that are discarded), while still being a haploid gamete. In flowering plants meiosis occurs in the **anthers** (pollen) and in the **ovules** (egg cell).

bullets: The two chromosomes in a pair can have **different alleles**.
Each pair separates **independently** of the others, by chance.
Number of possible combinations in humans: **2 to the power 23, about 8.4 million**, from independent assortment alone.
Fertilisation adds more variation because **any sperm** can fuse with **any egg**.
This explains why **siblings differ** (except identical twins, who come from one zygote splitting).
Beyond the spec: crossing over exchanges sections of chromosomes and increases variation further (not required, but a good extension).
Exam phrase: 'the gametes are genetically different because each contains a different mixture of alleles'.
core.h: Why the four gametes are all genetically different
core.p: The exam wants you to **explain** why gametes differ. There are two key sources. First, the chromosomes in a pair carry different alleles, and when the pairs separate in the first division, each pair lines up **randomly**, so which chromosome of each pair goes to which cell is a matter of **chance**. This is called **independent assortment**. Second, the alleles are reshuffled so that each gamete receives a unique mixture. Together this means that no two gametes (except by extreme chance) have the same combination of alleles.

bullets: Sperm n=23 + egg n=23 gives zygote 2n=46.
The zygote contains alleles from **both parents**.
Which sperm fertilises which egg is **random**, adding variation.
After fertilisation, cell division is by **mitosis**, so every cell of the embryo has the same DNA as the zygote.
The sex of the baby is decided at fertilisation by the sex chromosome carried by the sperm (X or Y).
Identical twins form when the early embryo splits into two; they are genetically identical.
core.h: Fertilisation and restoring the diploid number
core.p: At **fertilisation** the nucleus of a sperm (23 chromosomes) fuses with the nucleus of an egg (23 chromosomes) to give a **zygote** with **46 chromosomes**, 23 pairs. The two chromosomes in each pair come one from each parent, so the zygote has a new combination of genes. The zygote then divides by **mitosis**, making identical daughter cells, which **differentiate** to form tissues and organs of the new individual.

bullets: **Where**: mitosis in almost all body cells; meiosis only in reproductive organs.
**Divisions**: mitosis one division; meiosis two divisions.
**Number of cells**: 2 vs 4.
**Chromosome number**: stays 46 in mitosis; halves to 23 in meiosis.
**Genetic makeup**: identical in mitosis; different in meiosis.
**Purpose**: growth, repair, asexual reproduction vs making gametes for sexual reproduction.
**Similarity**: both start by **copying the DNA**.
core.p: A favourite question is to compare the two kinds of cell division. **Mitosis** makes **two** genetically **identical** diploid cells, for **growth, repair and asexual reproduction**. **Meiosis** makes **four** genetically **different** haploid cells and only occurs in the **reproductive organs** to make gametes. The key difference is what the daughter cells are like genetically, because that explains the different jobs.

bullets: Meiosis produces genetic variation in gametes.
Random fertilisation increases it further.
Variation can be **continuous** (height, mass) or **discontinuous** (blood group).
**Mutations** (changes in DNA) create entirely new alleles.
Variation allows natural selection and selective breeding.
The more genetically different the gametes, the more varied the offspring.
core.p: Variation between individuals comes from **genes** (inherited), the **environment**, or both. The variation caused by **meiosis and random fertilisation** is genetic, and it is the raw material that **natural selection** works on. A population with plenty of variation is more likely to contain individuals able to survive a new disease or climate change, so the species can adapt and evolve. A population with no variation (like clones) is at greater risk.

bullets: Accurate separation gives gametes with exactly one chromosome from each pair.
Non-disjunction means a pair fails to separate, giving gametes with 24 or 22 chromosomes.
Down's syndrome: 47 chromosomes (an extra chromosome 21).
The risk increases with the age of the mother.
Not required by the AQA spec, so use only if a question gives you the context.
Use as a link: errors in meiosis are one source of inherited-type disorders that are not passed by alleles.
core.p: Occasionally chromosomes fail to separate properly in meiosis, so that a gamete has too many or too few chromosomes. If such a gamete is fertilised, the zygote has the wrong total. For example, in **Down's syndrome** there are three copies of chromosome 21 (47 total). This is beyond the AQA GCSE requirements but is a powerful example showing why accurate separation matters.

bullets: Count the chromosomes; identify pairs by size and banding.
Meiosis: four cells, each with half the chromosomes, one from each pair.
Mitosis: two cells, each with the same chromosomes as the parent cell.
Possible combinations of chromosomes in a gamete from a cell with n pairs = **2^n** (n=2 gives 4, n=3 gives 8, n=23 gives 8 388 608).
If asked about genetic differences, say whether the cells are **identical or different**.
Draw the next stage lightly in pencil first, then label.
core.p: Questions often show a diagram of a cell with a few chromosomes and ask what the daughter cells look like. A good method: **count the chromosomes** in the starting cell, decide if the process is meiosis or mitosis, then work out the number and the types in the daughter cells. For meiosis the answer is **half the number**, with **one of each pair**. If asked how many different combinations, remember **2^n** for n pairs.

bullets: **Genetic inheritance and Punnett squares**: each gamete carries one allele.
**Inherited disorders and sex determination**: XX/XY split in meiosis.
**DNA and the genome**: what is replicated before meiosis.
**Natural selection**: needs variation that meiosis produces.
**Cloning**: no meiosis involved, so offspring are identical.
**Cell division (mitosis) in Paper 1**: compare and contrast.
core.p: Meiosis connects to nearly all of inheritance. The idea that each gamete contains **one allele** for each gene is what Punnett squares are built on; the **chance of inheriting an allele** comes from random fertilisation; **sex determination** depends on whether the sperm carries X or Y; **DNA structure** explains what is being copied; and **evolution** depends on variation from meiosis and mutation.

exam: **1 mark**: state where meiosis happens (testes/ovaries, anthers/ovules) or the number of chromosomes in a gamete (23).
**2 marks**: 'gametes have half the chromosomes' plus 'so fertilisation restores the diploid number'.
**3 to 4 marks, describe meiosis**: DNA copied; cell divides twice; four gametes; each has one set of chromosomes; all genetically different.
**Explain why gametes are different**: pairs separate randomly, each gamete gets a different mixture of alleles.
**Compare mitosis and meiosis**: use 'whereas'; give cell number, genetic makeup, chromosome number and purpose.
Diagram questions: count chromosomes first; meiosis gives half and one of each pair.
Calculation: possible gamete combinations = 2^n for n pairs; show the working.
Always include units/terms: 'haploid', 'diploid', 'chromosomes', not just 'half the cell'.
Link to variation: variation allows natural selection, so mention survival in a changing environment.

mistakes.r: Meiosis makes **four genetically different haploid** cells; mitosis makes two identical diploid cells.
Human gametes have **23** chromosomes (a single set).
Only in the **reproductive organs** (testes, ovaries, anthers, ovules).
mistakes.w: Meiosis happens in all body cells.

mistakes.r: They are **different from each other and from the parent**, with half the chromosomes.
mistakes.w: The gametes are the same as the parent cell.

mistakes.r: **Meiosis** halves it; **fertilisation restores** it to the diploid number.
Meiosis has **two divisions** after the DNA is copied.
The zygote divides by **mitosis** to grow.
Mainly because each gamete has a **different mixture of alleles** and fertilisation is random.
mistakes.w: Siblings are different because of the environment only.

summary: The spec asks you to describe meiosis: cells in the reproductive organs copy their genetic information and divide twice to form four genetically different gametes, each with a single set of chromosomes, and fertilisation restores the diploid number and mixes genes from two parents. It matters because it explains constant chromosome number across generations and the variation between offspring.

terms.d: A type of cell division in the reproductive organs that produces four genetically different haploid gametes.
A haploid sex cell (sperm, egg cell, pollen nucleus) that fuses at fertilisation.
Having a single set of chromosomes (23 in human gametes).
Having two sets of chromosomes (46 in human body cells).
A long molecule of coiled DNA in the nucleus carrying many genes.
A short section of DNA that codes for a protein and controls a characteristic.
A different version of the same gene.
The fusion of a male and a female gamete, restoring the diploid number.
The diploid cell formed when two gametes fuse.
Cell division producing two genetically identical diploid cells.
The entire genetic material of an organism.
Differences between individuals of a species, caused by genes, the environment or both.
The organs that make gametes: testes and ovaries in animals; anthers and ovules in flowering plants.
Two chromosomes in a pair that carry the same genes in the same places, one from each parent.
The random separation of chromosome pairs in meiosis so gametes get different mixtures of alleles.
The pair of chromosomes that determine sex: XX in females, XY in males.

worked.ans: Meiosis occurs in the reproductive organs. The genetic information in the cell is copied, then the cell divides twice to form four gametes. Each gamete has a single set of chromosomes (half the number of the original cell) and all four gametes are genetically different.
worked.q: Describe how meiosis produces gametes. (4 marks)
steps: Copy: the genetic information is copied.
Result: four gametes, each with a single set of chromosomes, all different.

worked.ans: Meiosis makes gametes that are genetically different because each has a different mixture of alleles. Fertilisation is random, so a different sperm and egg combination forms each child. The children therefore inherit different combinations of alleles (unless they are identical twins).
worked.q: Explain why a child is not identical to its brother or sister. (3 marks)
steps: Gametes from each parent are formed by meiosis and are all genetically different.
Which sperm fertilises which egg is random.
So each child gets a different mixture of alleles.

worked.q: A cell in a fly has 8 chromosomes. State the number of chromosomes in a gamete and the number of possible combinations of chromosomes in the gametes from independent assortment. (3 marks)
steps: Diploid number 8 = 4 pairs, so gametes have half: 4.
